documents: Chen & Li 2022, River Research and Applications 38:1775-1786, published paper (PDF)

entry.evidence: whether reservoirs have an important or minimal impact on the sediment and nutrients is far from conclusive

steps.action: Set conflicting published findings on whether reservoirs matter for basin sediment and nutrient loads against each other and posed the question as open.
steps.quote: whether reservoirs have an important or minimal impact on the sediment and nutrients is far from conclusive

steps.action: Took from the literature the rival expectations: large reservoirs dominate versus many small ones acting together, and reservoirs near river mouths being most effective (Bosch 2008).
steps.quote: the combination of many small reservoirs provides a greater reduction effect in nutrients than a single large one

steps.action: Stated three objectives: build a SWAT model with reservoirs for the MORB, assess reservoir reductions of loads, and evaluate the influence of reservoir size and location.
steps.quote: to evaluate the influence of reservoir's size and location on sediment and nutrient loads

steps.action: Built a basin-wide SWAT model (304 HUC8 sub-basins, 51,790 HRUs) with merged reservoirs (87), large/small classification, reservoir operation rules and aggregated ponds.
steps.quote: This study built a MORB SWAT model (a recently released version 2012.10_4.19) using ArcSWAT interface

steps.action: Calibrated streamflow parameters (manual snow step, then SUFI-2 autocalibration at six independent gauges) on 2007–2016 data, estimated TN and TP loads with LOADEST, and calibrated sediment and nutrient parameters manually.
steps.quote: were autocalibrated simultaneously by using the SWAT Calibration and Uncertainty Procedures

steps.action: Designed six scenarios: with all (WA) versus without reservoirs (WOA), size pair WL versus WUS1 with similar storage, and location pair WUS2 versus WDS with similar storage.
steps.quote: Six reservoir scenarios were run to assess how reservoirs' presence and absence as well as their sizes and locations may influence

steps.action: Validated the model against held-out 1997–2006 gauge records for streamflow, TSS, TN and TP, attributing poor NSE at Culbertson and Ashland to groundwater simulation and irrigation.
steps.quote: The simulated and measured streamflow and water quality in the MORB matched reasonably well for the calibration ( [...] validation (1997–2006) periods

steps.action: Compared WA and WOA runs at the basin outlet on annual, dry/wet-period and monthly scales for flow, TSS, TN and TP.
steps.quote: a greater reduction (11.9%) of the 20-year average TSS was found between the WA and WOA simulations

steps.action: Checked that moving the upstream/downstream division point downstream within 450 km does not change the main-stream conclusions (results not shown).
steps.quote: Overall conclusions would not change when a different location was chosen if it was moved downstream within a 450-km range (not shown).

steps.action: Mapped monthly percent changes of flow, TSS, TN and TP along the main stream between WA and WOA and attributed spatial patterns to reservoir trapping and channel processes.
steps.quote: TSS reduction induced by the reservoirs was greater (more than 70%) at the upstream section than that at the downstream section

steps.action: Computed trapping efficiencies at each dam and compared large and small reservoirs' mean TEs and shares of load reduction.
steps.quote: The mean TE values of TSS, TN, and TP due to the small reservoirs were 89.1%, 18.6%, and 25.7%

steps.action: Related dam trapping efficiencies to the ratio of reservoir surface area to reservoir flow, interpreting it as retention time.
steps.quote: High TEs were often found at the dams with higher ratios between RSA and RF

steps.action: Checked that choosing other comparison sites within 210 km of Omaha does not change the size and location results (results not shown).
steps.quote: Overall results would not change when different sites were selected within a 210-km range (not shown).

steps.action: Compared WL and WUS1 loads at Hermann and Omaha against the hypothesis that many small reservoirs equal one large one.
steps.quote: clearly supported the hypothesis that small reservoirs collectively could have equivalent effect on water quality as a large one

steps.action: Kept the claim that many small reservoirs reduce outlet loads as effectively as a large one, combining scenario and dam-site results.
steps.quote: many small reservoirs were effective in reducing sediment and nutrient loads at the MORB outlet in this study

steps.action: Compared WDS and WUS2 loads at Hermann: downstream reservoirs reduced more TSS but slightly less TN and TP, contrary to the Bosch (2008) expectation for nutrients.
steps.quote: By contrast, downstream small reservoirs' roles in reducing nutrients were weaker than those at the upstream in our study.

steps.action: Proposed that downstream reservoirs sit on tributaries outside the nutrient source area to explain the mismatch with the expected nutrient pattern.
steps.quote: Possible reason was that these downstream reservoirs were all located on the tributaries

steps.action: Checked the explanation by computing the Kansas and Osage watersheds' small shares of basin TN (13.4%) and TP (12.1%).
steps.quote: these two watersheds were not the source area of the nutrients

steps.action: Set the results against earlier studies: agreed with Wu and Liu (2012) against Seitzinger et al. (2002), and found some Bosch (2008) rules inapplicable in practice.
steps.quote: Results from this study agreed with the latter, that is, without considering the reservoirs' effects might lead to a large bias

steps.action: Refined the general rule: reservoir effects matter when reservoirs are in the nutrient source area or on the main stream, and reinterpreted Wu and Liu's small-reservoir result accordingly.
steps.quote: the reservoirs' role on water quality should be considered when they were in the source area of nutrients or on the main stream

steps.action: Concluded that reservoirs reduce outlet TSS, TN and TP by 11.9%, 7.6% and 14.6% (1997–2016), with effects varying by period, season, size and location.
steps.quote: the reservoirs greatly reduced sediment and nutrient export in the MORB

end.claim: Reservoirs reduced mean annual TSS, TN and TP loads at the MORB outlet by 11.9%, 7.6% and 14.6% during 1997–2016, with effects varying by reservoir size and location.

decisive_move.sentence: The counterfactual comparison of the calibrated model with all reservoirs (WA) and with reservoir operations disabled (WOA) produces every reduction figure; without it no claim exists.

gates.evidence: Observational data were existing USGS gauge records, not acquired under a hypothesis; the size and location scenarios were designed around literature hypotheses (p. 1778). The model faced held-out validation it could have failed (pp. 1778–1779), and the size hypothesis could have failed in the scenarios (p. 1782); the headline reduction estimates are counterfactual and untestable against data. Nothing is stated as fixed before the data, apart from the performance thresholds taken from Moriasi et al. (2015) and Santhi et al. (2014).

Fertilizer input data used as model input

novelty_claims.quote: the impacts of these reservoirs on water quality dynamics have not been systemically studied
The effect of these reservoirs on water quality and the influence of reservoirs' size and location on the fate and transport of sediments and nutrients [...]
This study was unique mainly because it focused on reservoirs induced water quality issue based on a modeling study of an actual river basin.

limits: No review file or earlier version was supplied, so the review sequence is not coded; the acknowledgments credit Dr. Yongping Yuan with suggestions on the scenario design and two anonymous reviewers, so step 6's author trigger may hide an outside contribution (inference). The reduction percentages carry no uncertainty ranges, and SWAT-CUP uncertainty output is not reported, so the estimate_with_resolution status is generous; resolution is limited to the gauge-level fit statistics. The model was calibrated only with reservoirs present (WA); the WOA counterfactual is never checked against data (inference). Both robustness checks on comparison locations are reported as 'not shown'. Reservoir inflow and outflow data were unavailable (p. 1784), and the authors note that the limited number of observation sites adds regional uncertainty. Several nutrient NSE values are low or negative (Table 3), yet the fit is judged satisfactory on PBIAS. Sub-claim statuses: small reservoirs collectively equivalent to a large one is best_explanation (scenario support, no independent test); downstream reservoirs reduce more TSS but less TN and TP is best_explanation, with a post hoc source-area explanation; the TE versus RSA/RF relation is an informal regularity without a fitted range. Composition is none_fits because the walk is calibrate, then validate, then run model counterfactual scenarios; it matches no listed composition, and the conditions are set in a model, not found or set in nature. Data are available only upon request.

disagreements.target: Seitzinger et al. (2002); Rajib and Merwade (2017); studies that ignore or simplify reservoirs
disagreements.support: Basin-scale WA versus WOA simulation shows 7.6–14.6% outlet load reductions and mean dam TEs of 18.9–93.1%, so ignoring reservoirs would bias models.
disagreements.quote: Results from this study agreed with the latter, that is, without considering the reservoirs' effects might lead to a large bias in the model [...] .

disagreements.target: Bosch (2008) rules from a hypothetical reservoir basin (reservoirs near the river mouth most effective; many small reservoirs stronger than one large)
disagreements.support: In the WDS versus WUS2 scenarios, downstream reservoirs reduced more TSS but 0.5% less TN and 1.6% less TP than upstream ones, which the authors attribute to source-area location.
disagreements.quote: But some rules might not be applicable in practice.

disagreements.target: Wu and Liu (2012) on small-reservoir reduction effects
disagreements.support: The authors supply the missing explanation: the Coralville Reservoir lies on the main stream near the river mouth, so it affects almost all nutrients in the basin.
disagreements.quote: However, they did not explain the reason.
